tip: 'Auf-' as a separable prefix often means 'up' or 'open' ('aufstehen', 'aufmachen') – it goes to the sentence end.
'Nach' also means 'after' in time and takes the dative: 'nach ihrer Ausbildung' = after her training.
After a question word like 'wann', the verb moves to the end: 'wann der nächste Zug abfährt'.
'Dürfte ich' is an extra-polite 'may I', one notch softer than 'darf ich': 'dürfte ich bitte die Speisekarte sehen' is a very gentle way to ask.
Here 'in dem' means 'where' and starts a relative clause, so the verb goes last: 'in dem wir uns kennengelernt haben'.
'Moin' is used in northern Germany at any time of day.
For a break German uses 'machen', not 'nehmen': 'eine Pause machen' (take a break).
'Gratulieren' takes a plain dative object: 'gratulieren unserem Onkel' (congratulate our uncle).
'Verzeihen' takes a dative object, as if you forgive to someone: 'meinem Bruder' (my brother).
'Einladen' splits: the prefix 'ein' moves to the clause end, 'laden ... ein' (invite).
'Name' is a special noun that takes '-n' outside the subject form: 'deinen Namen' (your name).
'Lesen' shifts 'e' to 'ie' in the 'du' and 'er/sie' forms: 'sie liest' (she reads).
After 'einen', a masculine accusative adjective ends in '-en': 'einen langen Bericht'.
'Tragen' adds an umlaut in the 'er/sie' form, 'a' to 'ä': 'er trägt' (he carries).
After 'das', the adjective ends in '-e': 'das blaue Hemd' (the blue shirt).
'Vertrauen' takes a dative object: 'vertraue meinem besten Freund' (trust my best friend).
A helper like 'kann' sends the main verb to the clause end in its basic form: 'kann ... helfen'.
Dative plural nouns normally add '-n': 'unseren Gästen' (to our guests), from 'die Gäste'.
'Folgen' takes the dative, not the accusative: 'folgt dem Rat' (follows the advice).
'Einen Heiratsantrag machen' ('gemacht' here) literally means 'make a proposal', the set phrase for 'to propose'.
An accusative with no preposition can mark how long something lasts: 'den ganzen Abend' (all evening long).
Formal commands keep 'Sie' right after the verb: 'rufen Sie ... an'.
'Suchen' needs no word for 'for'; it takes a direct object: 'sucht ihre Schlüssel' (searches for her keys).
With a separable verb, 'zu' goes between prefix and stem: 'anzufangen' (to start).
'Ähneln' takes the dative: 'ähnelt seinem Großvater' (resembles his grandfather).
'Gefallen' flips subject and object: 'sie gefällt ihrem Freund' means her boyfriend likes her.
'Gratulieren' marks the occasion with 'zu' ('zum' = 'zu' + 'dem'): 'gratuliere dir zum Erfolg' (on the success).
Days take 'am', a contraction of 'an dem': 'am Sonntag' (on Sunday).
For cities and most countries, travel uses 'nach': 'nach Wien' (to Vienna).
'Jemanden lieb haben' is a set phrase for being fond of someone: 'hat seinen Hund lieb'.
